chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Gold Standard Era and the Fall of the British Pound

lessons.title: Bretton Woods: Building a New Monetary Order in 1944

body.text: Three weeks after D-Day, with the war still raging, 44 nations sat down in a New Hampshire hotel and designed the monetary system the entire world would run on for the next three decades, built openly around one currency: the US dollar.

children.text: Lesson 2 left sterling weakened by two world wars and the dollar clearly in the ascendant. In July 1944, that shift was made official. Delegates from 44 Allied nations gathered at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to design a monetary system for the postwar world, one that would avoid both the rigidity that had crippled the classical gold standard in Lesson 1 and the chaotic competitive devaluations of the 1930s covered in Lesson 2. What they built lasted, in its original form, until 1971.
Two Competing Visions: White vs Keynes

markDefs.definition: A proposed international reserve currency put forward by John Maynard Keynes at Bretton Woods, to be issued by a new International Clearing Union rather than tied to any single nation's currency or to gold directly.

children.text: Two rival plans dominated the negotiations. John Maynard Keynes, representing an exhausted Britain, proposed an International Clearing Union built around a new supranational reserve asset he called

, designed so that both countries running large surpluses and countries running large deficits would face pressure to adjust, not deficit countries alone. Harry Dexter White, representing the United States Treasury, proposed a simpler system centred on the dollar itself, backed by a more limited fund that countries could borrow from temporarily during balance of payments trouble. The two plans reflected two very different positions of power, and only one delegation was negotiating from a position of overwhelming financial strength.

body.title: The Keynes Plan vs the White Plan

columns.label: Keynes Plan (Britain)
points: A new international reserve currency, bancor, issued by a global clearing union
Symmetric pressure on both surplus and deficit countries to adjust
No single national currency sits at the centre of the system
A larger pool of resources to support countries in balance of payments difficulty

columns.label: White Plan (United States)
points: The US dollar, convertible to gold, sits at the centre of the system
Adjustment pressure falls mainly on deficit countries
A more limited fund, the future International Monetary Fund, with fixed national quotas
Reflected America's position as the dominant creditor and gold holder

body.text: The outcome was never really in doubt. The United States held roughly two-thirds of the world's official monetary gold by 1944, largely because Allied nations had spent the war years paying America in gold for war materiel, and it was the only major economy to emerge from the war physically undamaged. Keynes's bancor plan was intellectually influential, and elements of it resurface decades later in debates about the IMF's own Special Drawing Rights, but the country with the gold and the untouched factories set the terms. The White Plan won.

children.text: The System That Was Actually Built

markDefs.definition: The Bretton Woods exchange rate system: currencies were fixed to the US dollar within narrow bands, but unlike the rigid classical gold standard, a country could formally adjust its peg with IMF approval if it faced a fundamental balance of payments problem.

children.text: The agreed system fixed the US dollar to gold at $35 an ounce, and fixed every other member currency to the dollar within narrow bands, an arrangement known as the

. Only foreign central banks and governments, not private citizens or companies, could convert dollars into gold at that fixed rate. In effect, the dollar became as good as gold for the rest of the world's central banks, which is precisely why they were willing to hold it as their primary reserve asset. Two new institutions were created to run and support the system.

children.text: India at the Table, Still a Colony

British India was one of the 44 founding signatories at Bretton Woods, and later a founding member of both the IMF and the World Bank, three full years before independence in 1947. That seat at the table was not incidental. Lesson 2 covered how India had emerged from the Second World War as one of Britain's largest creditors, holding sterling balances worth roughly £1.3 billion. A colony that size, with that much financial weight, could not simply be left out of a conference designing the postwar monetary order, even while it remained under colonial rule and had no independent foreign policy of its own.

body.text: Sit with that contradiction for a moment. India helped shape the rules of the postwar monetary system it would inherit as an independent nation just three years later, while still being governed from London. Its early relationship with the IMF and World Bank, institutions this course refers back to repeatedly, dates from before India was even sovereign.

children.text: The Bretton Woods system solved the rigidity problem of the classical gold standard, but it inherited a version of the exorbitant privilege and Triffin's dilemma covered in Chapter 1, before either term had even been coined. Every country outside the US needed dollars to hold as reserves and use in trade, which meant the US had to run balance of payments deficits to actually supply the world with them. But the more dollars the US sent abroad relative to its own gold stock, the harder it became to credibly promise that every one of those dollars could still be converted to gold at $35 an ounce on demand. That tension sat quietly under the system for over two decades before it finally broke it, the subject Chapter 3 opens with.

body.title: Before You Move to Chapter 3
steps: Write down, in one sentence each, the core difference between the Keynes Plan and the White Plan
Note the fixed gold price the dollar was pegged to, and think about what would need to be true for the US to honour that promise forever
Recall Triffin's dilemma from Chapter 1, Lesson 2, and try to state in your own words why Bretton Woods was vulnerable to the same problem
Move to Chapter 3, which opens with the Nixon Shock of 1971 and the collapse of the gold-dollar link this lesson describes

body.title: Negotiating From Keynes's Seat
body.scenario: You are part of the British delegation at Bretton Woods in July 1944. Your own proposal, the bancor and the International Clearing Union, would spread reserve currency responsibilities across a new global institution rather than concentrating them in the US dollar. The American delegation, backed by two-thirds of the world's gold and a war-strengthened economy, is unwilling to accept anything that does not place the dollar at the centre.
body.prompt: Given what this lesson covered about the balance of financial power in 1944, was the Keynes Plan ever likely to succeed at that specific conference? What would have had to be different for it to have a real chance?
body.modelAnswer: Realistically, no. Bretton Woods was not a negotiation between equals; it was a negotiation between a nation that held most of the world's gold and an untouched industrial base, and a nation that had just spent Lesson 2's two wars borrowing, devaluing, and running down its own reserves. For the Keynes Plan to have had a real chance, the balance of financial power itself would have needed to be different, either a less financially dominant United States, or a coalition of other creditor nations willing to back a shared reserve asset instead of the dollar. Ideas rarely beat leverage at a table like this one; the delegation holding the gold and the factories set the terms, which is exactly the pattern Chapter 1 described for why reserve currency status is earned through underlying economic weight, not simply argued for.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Under the Bretton Woods system agreed in 1944, who could convert US dollars into gold at the fixed $35 an ounce rate?
options: Any private citizen or company, anywhere in the world
Only foreign central banks and governments
Only the United States Federal Reserve itself
No one; gold convertibility had already been abolished by 1944
body.explanation: Only foreign central banks and governments could convert dollars to gold at the fixed $35 an ounce rate, not private individuals or companies. This made the dollar effectively as good as gold for the official institutions that mattered most to the system, while everyday holders of dollars had no such direct gold conversion right.

body.text: Dates, figures, and institutional details about the Bretton Woods conference, including gold reserve shares, the fixed gold price, and the founding member count, are presented as widely cited historical facts and approximations for teaching purposes. This lesson is educational content on monetary history, not investment advice.

points: The July 1944 Bretton Woods conference, attended by 44 Allied nations, designed the postwar monetary system around the US dollar rather than Keynes's proposed international reserve currency, bancor
The White Plan won largely because the US held roughly two-thirds of the world's official gold by 1944 and had an industrial base untouched by the war, giving it decisive negotiating leverage
The agreed system fixed the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce and fixed other currencies to the dollar under an adjustable peg, with only foreign central banks able to convert dollars to gold

The conference created the IMF and the IBRD, later the World Bank; British India was a founding member of both while still under colonial rule, a direct result of the sterling balances covered in Lesson 2

The system inherited an early version of Triffin's dilemma from Chapter 1: supplying the world with dollars required persistent US deficits, a tension that would eventually break the system, the subject Chapter 3 opens with
